title: Transcendentalism
wiki_lead:
Transcendentalism is a philosophical, spiritual, literary movement that was developed in the late 1820s and 1830s in the New England region of the United States. A core belief is in the inherent goodness of people and nature, and while society and its institutions have corrupted the purity of the individual, people are at their best when truly "self-reliant" and independent. Transcendentalists saw divine experience inherent in the everyday. They thought of physical and spiritual phenomena as part of dynamic processes rather than as discrete entities.
Transcendentalism is one of the first philosophical currents that emerged in the United States; it is therefore a key early point in the history of American philosophy. Emphasizing subjective intuition over objective empiricism, its adherents believe that individuals are capable of generating completely original insights with little attention and deference to past transcendentalists. Its rise was a protest against the general state of intellectualism and spirituality at the time. The doctrine of the Unitarian church as taught at Harvard Divinity School was closely related.
Transcendentalism was thought to originally have emerged from "English and German Romanticism, the Biblical criticism of Johann Gottfried Herder and Friedrich Schleiermacher, the skepticism of David Hume", and the transcendental philosophy of Immanuel Kant and German idealism. Perry Miller and Arthur Versluis regard Emanuel Swedenborg and Jakob Böhme as pervasive influences on transcendentalism.

Origin
Transcendentalism is closely related to Unitarianism in Boston in the early nineteenth century. It started to develop after Unitarianism took hold at Harvard University, following the elections of Henry Ware as the Hollis Professor of Divinity in 1805 and of John Thornton Kirkland as President in 1810. Transcendentalism was not a rejection of Unitarianism; rather, it developed as an organic consequence of the Unitarian emphasis on free conscience and the value of intellectual reason. The transcendentalists were not content with the sobriety, mildness, and calm rationalism of Unitarianism. Instead, they wanted a more intense spiritual experience. Thus, transcendentalism was not born as a counter-movement to Unitarianism, but as a parallel movement to the very ideas introduced by the Unitarians.


Transcendental Club

Transcendentalism became a coherent movement and a sacred organization with the founding of the Transcendental Club in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on September 12, 1836, by prominent New England intellectuals, including George Putnam, Ralph Waldo Emerson, and Frederic Henry Hedge. Other members of the club included Sophia Ripley, Margaret Fuller, Elizabeth Peabody, Ellen Sturgis Hooper, Caroline Sturgis Tappan, Amos Bronson Alcott, Orestes Brownson, Theodore Parker, Henry David Thoreau, William Henry Channing, James Freeman Clarke, Christopher Pearse Cranch, Convers Francis, Sylvester Judd, Jones Very, and Charles Stearns
grok_lead: Transcendentalism was a philosophical, literary, and reform movement that arose in the United States during the 1830s and 1840s, primarily among New England intellectuals dissatisfied with the rationalism of Unitarianism and empiricism, and influenced by European Romanticism. It asserted the primacy of intuition and individual conscience over sensory experience and institutional authority, positing that humans could access divine truths through direct insight into nature and the self. Central to the movement was a belief in the inherent goodness of both humanity and the natural world, rejecting materialism and advocating self-reliance as pathways to spiritual fulfillment. Ralph Waldo Emerson's 1836 essay Nature served as a foundational text, articulating the idea that the universe reflects an Oversoul uniting all existence, while Henry David Thoreau's Walden (1854) exemplified transcendentalist principles through his experiment in simple living at Walden Pond. Margaret Fuller contributed through her editorship of The Dial, the movement's periodical, and her advocacy for women's intellectual equality in Woman in the Nineteenth Century (1845). Though short-lived as a formal group, Transcendentalism influenced American literature, environmental ethics, and social reforms like abolitionism by prioritizing personal moral agency over collective dogma, yet its idealism has faced criticism for underestimating human self-interest and societal constraints evident in historical data on conflict and inequality.
